---
title: Multi-tenancy
description: How Vaulter fits into a multi-tenant Laravel app — the host-owned tenant_id column, swapping in a tenant-aware model, and aligning ulid morphs with the Corex / AzGuard ecosystem.
outline: deep
---

# Multi-tenancy

Vaulter is built to drop into a multi-tenant application, but it takes a deliberate
stance: **the host owns tenancy, Vaulter never scopes by it.** Vaulter gives you a
`tenant_id` column on its tables and threads its value through the content-addressed
store; *applying* a tenant scope — making queries see only one tenant's rows — is
your application's job, done by swapping in a tenant-aware model.

::: info The one rule
> Vaulter does not scope by `tenant_id`. Supply a tenant-aware model (via the
> `models` config) that applies your scope.
>
> — `config/vaulter.php`, the `tenant` block

This keeps Vaulter compatible with *any* tenancy strategy — single database with a
discriminator column, a tenancy package, or your own global scopes — instead of
hard-coding one.
:::

## Enabling tenancy

```php
// config/vaulter.php
'tenant' => [
    'enabled' => env('VAULTER_TENANT_ENABLED', false),
    'column'  => 'tenant_id',
],
```

- `tenant.enabled` — the global flag, read by `Config::tenantEnabled()`.
- `tenant.column` — the column name, read by `Config::tenantColumn()` (defaults to
  `tenant_id`).

### A note on the `tenant_id` column

The Drive tables (`v_storages`, `v_nodes`, `v_blobs`, `v_files`, …) **always** carry
a nullable `tenant_id` column, regardless of `tenant.enabled`. This is intentional:
the blob dedup-UNIQUE index keys on `tenant_id` under `dedup.scope = tenant`, so the
column must exist for the index to be defined. When tenancy is off, the index simply
spans a `NULL` column.

```php
// Vaulter\Schema\SchemaBuilder::tenant() — runs for every Drive table
private function tenant(Blueprint $table, IdStrategy $ids): void
{
    $ids->reference(table: $table, column: 'tenant_id', nullable: true);
}
```

The model property is declared on every Drive model
(`Vaulter\Models\Drive\Drive`, `Node`, `File`, `FileRevision`,
`Vaulter\Models\Cas\Blob`, `Vaulter\Models\Access\NodeGrant`,
`Vaulter\Models\Sharing\NodeShare`, …) as `int|string|null $tenant_id`.

::: tip
The `tenant.enabled` flag is what *your* tenant-aware models and migrations should
key on. Vaulter reads it only to decide whether to apply the optional column on the
**legacy DocVault** tables (`Vaulter\Schema\VaulterSchema::tenant()` is conditional);
the modern Drive tables emit the column unconditionally as explained above.
:::

## How `tenant_id` actually flows

Because Vaulter never scopes, it also never *invents* a tenant id. Watch where the
value comes from:

```
your tenant-aware Storage model
        │  sets tenant_id on create (a `creating` observer, a global scope, …)
        ▼
   v_storages.tenant_id
        │  IngestFileAction reads $storage->tenant_id
        ▼
   BlobStore::commit(tenantId: …)
        │  bakes it into the scope segment + dedup key
        ▼
   v_blobs.tenant_id  +  storage_key "t<id>/ab/cd/<sha256>"
```

The provisioning path proves the point — `DriveProvisioner::provision()` creates a
storage **without** a `tenant_id`:

```php
// Vaulter\Drive\DriveProvisioner::provision() — no tenant_id is set here
$storage = $this->store->create([
    'panel'        => $panel,
    'owner_type'   => $owner->getMorphClass(),
    'owner_id'     => $owner->getKey(),
    'name'         => $this->defaultName($owner),
    'disk'         => Config::defaultDisk(),
    'storage_type' => $this->storageType($panel),
    'used_bytes'   => 0,
]);
```

If you want `tenant_id` populated, your swapped-in `Storage` model must set it. From
there it propagates automatically: `Vaulter\Drive\Actions\Files\IngestFileAction` reads it
straight off the storage row and hands it to the blob store:

```php
// Vaulter\Drive\Actions\Files\IngestFileAction
$blob = $this->blobs->commit(
    stream:    $data->stream,
    tenantId:  $data->storage->tenant_id,   // ← from the storage row, host-populated
    storageId: $data->storage->id,
    disk:      $data->storage->disk,
);
```

The same pattern holds elsewhere: `Vaulter\Activity\ActivityRecorder` and
`Vaulter\Uploads\UploadSessionManager` both copy `tenant_id` off the owning
storage/node, never from a global Vaulter setting.

## Swapping in a tenant-aware model

The mechanism is the `models` map. Point any entry at your own subclass and Vaulter
resolves the model through that map everywhere:

```php
// config/vaulter.php
'models' => [
    // …
    'storage' => \App\Models\Vaulter\TenantStorage::class,
    'node'    => \App\Models\Vaulter\TenantNode::class,
    'blob'    => \App\Models\Vaulter\TenantBlob::class,
    // …
],
```

A minimal tenant-aware storage that *stamps and scopes* by the current tenant:

```php
namespace App\Models\Vaulter;

use Illuminate\Database\Eloquent\Builder;
use Vaulter\Models\Drive\Drive as BaseStorage;

class TenantStorage extends BaseStorage
{
    protected static function booted(): void
    {
        // Stamp the tenant on create — this is the value that flows into blobs.
        static::creating(function (self $storage): void {
            $storage->tenant_id ??= tenant()?->getKey();
        });

        // Scope reads to the current tenant — the part Vaulter deliberately omits.
        static::addGlobalScope('tenant', function (Builder $query): void {
            if ($tenantId = tenant()?->getKey()) {
                $query->where('tenant_id', $tenantId);
            }
        });
    }
}
```

::: tip Reach for an existing tenancy package
`tenant()` above is a stand-in. If you use a tenancy package (e.g. one that already
provides a `BelongsToTenant` trait and a current-tenant resolver), apply *its* trait
to your subclass instead of hand-rolling the scope. Vaulter does not care *how* the
scope is applied — only that the model applies one.
:::

Because the models are swappable and the `tenant_id` column already exists, you add
tenant isolation **without a Vaulter migration or core change** — the layer-mirror
of [the swappable-models design](/guide/configuration#models).

## Interplay with the dedup scope

Tenancy and the [content-addressed store](/guide/storage-and-blobs) meet at one
setting: `dedup.scope`.

```php
// config/vaulter.php
'dedup' => [
    'scope' => env('VAULTER_DEDUP_SCOPE', 'tenant'), // global|tenant|storage
],
```

For a multi-tenant install the default `tenant` is almost always what you want:

| `dedup.scope` | Behaviour in a multi-tenant app |
|---|---|
| `tenant` *(default)* | `UNIQUE (tenant_id, sha256)`. Identical bytes are stored **once per tenant**. No cross-tenant **existence leak** — tenant A can never learn that tenant B holds a given file. The `storage_key` is prefixed `t<id>/…`, so one tenant's GC can never touch another's bytes. |
| `global` | `UNIQUE (sha256)`. Bytes are deduplicated **across tenants** — cheaper storage, but a tenant could infer another tenant holds identical bytes. Choose only when that is acceptable. |
| `storage` | `UNIQUE (storage_id, sha256)`. Dedup is per storage container, a tighter boundary than per tenant. |

::: warning Pick the scope at install time
`dedup.scope` is baked into every blob's `storage_key` **and** the unique index. It
is effectively a one-way door — changing it later means rewriting keys and the index.
For tenant isolation with no existence leak, keep it at `tenant`.
:::

::: details Why `tenant` prevents an existence leak
Under `global` dedup, the first uploader of some bytes creates the object; a second
tenant uploading the *same* bytes gets a dedup hit and stores nothing — observable
through timing/accounting, which leaks that *someone* already holds those bytes.
Under `tenant` dedup the second tenant gets its own physical object, so there is
nothing to observe. The scope segment in the key (`t<id>/…`) makes this concrete on
disk.
:::

## Aligning ulid morphs with Corex / AzGuard

Vaulter defaults its primary-key strategy to **ulid** precisely so its morph keys
line up with the Corex / AzGuard ecosystem:

```php
// config/vaulter.php
'ids' => [
    'default' => env('VAULTER_ID_STRATEGY', 'ulid'), // ulid|uuid7|bigint (D9)
    // …
],
```

> Default is ulid so morph keys line up with the Corex/Azgard ecosystem.
> — `config/vaulter.php`, the `ids` block

This matters when you run the **AzGuard host-role driver** for authorization in a
tenant-scoped app. That driver
(`Vaulter\Azgard\AzgardPermissionDriver`) talks only to the
Vaulter-owned `Vaulter\Azgard\Contracts\AzgardGuard` seam — so vaulter-core carries
**no** hard dependency on `azguard` / `corex` — and routes its workspace-scoped role
checks through `hasPermissionIn($contextType, $contextId, $permission)`, which is
the Corex `TenantContextGuard` contextual check (the tenant/workspace lane).

For those morph types to resolve correctly across packages, the host must align the
ulid morph configuration end to end:

```dotenv
# Vaulter
VAULTER_ID_STRATEGY=ulid

# AzGuard
AZ_GUARD_MORPH_TYPE=ulid
```

```php
// Corex
'ids' => ['strategy' => \Corex\…\Ulid::class],   // corex.ids.strategy = Ulid
```

…and register the workspace / owner morph types as **Corex morph aliases**
(`EntityRegistry` / Corex ADR-003), as documented on the `AzgardGuard` contract:

```php
// Vaulter\Azgard\Contracts\AzgardGuard (docblock)
// The $contextType / $entity morph types MUST be registered Corex morph aliases
// aligned with vaulter.ids.default=ulid + corex.ids.strategy=Ulid + AZ_GUARD_MORPH_TYPE=ulid.
```

::: info Install the AzGuard bridge
`composer require axioma-studio/vaulter-azgard` installs the driver, real adapter and
`Vaulter\Azgard\Testing\FakeAzgardGuard`. Its provider registers the driver and binds
the guard; the user model must implement `Vaulter\Azgard\Contracts\AzgardBackedUser`.
Fake-based tests require the bridge's installed dependencies too. See
[Permission drivers](/guide/permission-drivers) and the `vaulter-azgard.*` configuration.
:::

## Putting it together

A typical tenant-scoped Vaulter install:

1. Set `tenant.enabled = true` and keep `tenant.column = 'tenant_id'`.
2. Keep `dedup.scope = tenant` so blobs are isolated per tenant with no existence
   leak.
3. Subclass the Vaulter models you need to scope (at least `storage`; usually `node`,
   `file`, `blob`, `activity`) and point the `models` map at them. Each subclass
   stamps `tenant_id` on create and applies your global scope.
4. If you use AzGuard for authorization, keep `ids.default = ulid` and align the
   Corex / AzGuard morph configuration as above.

From there, every upload threads the tenant through to its blob automatically, and
your model layer — not Vaulter — enforces what each tenant can see.

## See also

- [Storage & Blobs](/guide/storage-and-blobs) — the content-addressed store the
  `tenant_id` and `dedup.scope` feed into.
- [Configuration](/guide/configuration) — the full `tenant`, `dedup`, `ids` and
  `models` keys.
- [Authorization › Host role driver](/guide/permission-drivers) — the AzGuard driver and
  the `vaulter-azgard.*` configuration.

---
title: Permission Drivers
description: The four PermissionDriver lanes — Database (default), Gate, Spatie v8 teams, and the AzGuard seam — how to select and configure each, and the separate bridge’s AzgardGuard adapter.
outline: deep
---

# Permission Drivers

The [`AccessResolver`](./authorization) owns the per-node ACL and the final decision.
The **role lane** it folds in is swappable: it is the `PermissionDriver` contract, and
Core ships `database`, `gate` and `spatie`; the separate bridge supplies `azgard`. This is where you bridge your application's identity
and role system into Vaulter.

::: info The contract is node-blind
A `PermissionDriver` never receives a `Node` and never deals in magic-string actions —
only an `Authorizable` actor and an `AccessScope` (panel + workspace coordinates + node
owner). That keeps every driver swappable and the resolver the single authority.
:::

## The PermissionDriver contract

`Vaulter\Contracts\Access\PermissionDriver`:

```php
interface PermissionDriver
{
    // Per-subject role decision, or null when the host has nothing to say.
    // Folded as roleAllow into granted = max(aclAllow, roleAllow) — it can RAISE
    // access but never override a deny (the final veto still applies).
    public function resolve(Subject $subject, Authorizable $actor, AccessScope $scope): ?Decision;

    // An absolute super-admin override, or null. Allow/Deny short-circuit BOTH
    // directions before any ACL walk.
    public function override(Authorizable $actor, AccessScope $scope): ?Effect;

    // Expand an actor into the Subjects whose grants apply (user + roles + teams).
    // Vaulter builds WHERE (subject_type, subject_id) IN (...) from this list.
    /** @return list<Subject> */
    public function subjectsFor(Authorizable $actor): array;

    // May the actor create nodes in a workspace? (folder/upload create path).
    public function canCreateInWorkspace(Authorizable $actor, string $workspaceType, int|string $workspaceId): bool;
}
```

A driver's `resolve()` may only **raise** access (it returns an allow `Decision` or
`null`); the deny veto stays the ACL's job. `subjectsFor()` is what lets a
`v_node_grants` row addressed to a role or team match an actor.

## Selecting a driver

The active driver is a single config key (and env var):

```php
// config/vaulter.php
'drivers' => [
    'permission' => env('VAULTER_PERMISSION_DRIVER', 'database'),
],
```

```bash
# .env
VAULTER_PERMISSION_DRIVER=database   # database | gate | spatie | azgard | null
```

The key → FQCN map is `permission_drivers`. Register your own driver by adding an FQCN
that implements `PermissionDriver` (config-cache safe — FQCNs only, no closures):

```php
// config/vaulter.php
'permission_drivers' => [
    'database' => \Vaulter\Access\Drivers\DatabasePermissionDriver::class,
    'gate'     => \Vaulter\Access\Drivers\GatePermissionDriver::class,
    'spatie'   => \Vaulter\Access\Drivers\SpatiePermissionDriver::class,
    'null'     => \Vaulter\Testing\NullPermissionDriver::class, // non-prod only
    // 'tenant' => \App\Vaulter\TenantRoleDriver::class,
],
```

The `PermissionDriverManager` resolves and memoises the driver per key; an unknown key
throws `MissingPermissionDriverException::unknownDriver()`, and `null` in production throws
`nullDriverInProduction()` — see [Authorization → fail-loud](./authorization#fail-loud-the-null-driver).

## Database — the default, standalone lane

`Vaulter\Access\Drivers\DatabasePermissionDriver` introduces **no** external role
system. Every decision is a `v_node_grants` row resolved by the `AccessResolver`; the
driver only contributes the actor's own identity to the subject-set.

| Method | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `subjectsFor` | `[Subject::ofModel($actor)]` — just the user. |
| `override` | `null` — no super-admin bypass. |
| `resolve` | `null` — the ACL is the sole authority. |
| `canCreateInWorkspace` | `true` — per-node `CREATE` grants on the destination still apply via the resolver. |

This is the out-of-the-box lane that makes Vaulter work in a clean Laravel app with no
host authorization. To add role/team subjects without any external package, subclass it
and append `Subject` entries:

```php
final class TeamAwareRoleDriver extends DatabasePermissionDriver
{
    public function subjectsFor(Authorizable $actor): array
    {
        $subjects = parent::subjectsFor($actor); // [Subject(user)]

        foreach ($actor->teams as $team) {
            $subjects[] = new Subject(type: 'team', id: $team->id);
        }

        return $subjects;
    }
}
```

## Gate — Laravel's built-in lane

`Vaulter\Access\Drivers\GatePermissionDriver` bridges a host that already
authorizes through Gate abilities / policies. It ships with the framework — zero extra
dependencies.

- **`override`** asks a configurable super ability (default `vaulter.super`). When the
  Gate allows it, the actor short-circuits to full access; otherwise it defers (`null`,
  never a hard deny).
- **`resolve`** asks the Gate each mapped ability (low → high) and folds the **highest
  allowed level** into the `Decision`. The Gate check is node-blind — it receives the
  `AccessScope`'s `{panel, workspace_type, workspace_id}`, never a `Node`.
- **`subjectsFor`** = `[Subject(actor)]` only. The Gate exposes no enumerable role/team
  subjects, so grant rows addressed to a role/team are not matched by this lane — use
  Spatie/AzGuard for that.
- **`canCreateInWorkspace`** asks the create ability, passed `[$workspaceType, $workspaceId]`.

Every check goes through `Gate::forUser($actor)`, so the driver is stateless. A missing
ability is swallowed as "not allowed" — an unconfigured host gate never throws into the
resolver.

### Configuration

```php
// config/vaulter.php — used only when drivers.permission = 'gate'
'gate' => [
    'abilities' => [
        'reader'    => 'vaulter.view',
        'commenter' => 'vaulter.comment',
        'writer'    => 'vaulter.edit',
        'organizer' => 'vaulter.organize',
        'owner'     => 'vaulter.manage',
    ],
    'super_ability'  => env('VAULTER_GATE_SUPER_ABILITY', 'vaulter.super'),
    'create_ability' => env('VAULTER_GATE_CREATE_ABILITY', 'vaulter.create'),
],
```

The `abilities` map couples a Vaulter `GrantLevel` to a host Gate ability string. Map
only the levels you actually gate. Implement matching policies:

```php
// A host policy / Gate definition
Gate::define('vaulter.edit', fn ($user, array $context) =>
    $user->isEditorOf($context['workspace_type'], $context['workspace_id']));

Gate::define('vaulter.super', fn ($user) => $user->isAdmin());

Gate::define('vaulter.create', fn ($user, string $type, int|string $id) =>
    $user->mayCreateIn($type, $id));
```

## Spatie — roles, permissions, and v8 teams

`Vaulter\Access\Drivers\SpatiePermissionDriver` bridges a host running
`spatie/laravel-permission`, including the **v8 teams** feature. It encapsulates the
entire v8 team-switch dance so it never leaks into the resolver.

- **`subjectsFor`** = the actor + its role Subjects (+ its team Subject when teams are
  enabled), so a grant row addressed to a `role`/`team` matches.
- **`resolve`** checks each mapped permission via `$actor->hasPermissionTo($name)`,
  **team-scoped** to the workspace (`setPermissionsTeamId($scope->workspaceId)`), then
  restores the previous team id and the actor's loaded relations. The highest allowed
  level becomes the `Decision`.
- **`override`** asks a configurable super permission.
- **`canCreateInWorkspace`** asks the create permission in the workspace's team context.

::: warning Optional dependency
`spatie/laravel-permission` is an **optional** host dependency. Every runtime touch of
the Spatie API is guarded by `class_exists(PermissionRegistrar::class)`, so vaulter-core
carries no hard dependency. Selecting `spatie` without installing the package degrades
to a safe deny (`null`/`false`), never a fatal error.
:::

### Configuration

```php
// config/vaulter.php — used only when drivers.permission = 'spatie'
'spatie' => [
    'permissions' => [
        'reader'    => 'vaulter.view',
        'commenter' => 'vaulter.comment',
        'writer'    => 'vaulter.edit',
        'organizer' => 'vaulter.organize',
        'owner'     => 'vaulter.manage',
    ],
    'super_permission'  => env('VAULTER_SPATIE_SUPER_PERMISSION', 'vaulter.super'),
    'create_permission' => env('VAULTER_SPATIE_CREATE_PERMISSION', 'vaulter.create'),
    'teams'             => env('VAULTER_SPATIE_TEAMS', false),
    'role_subject_type' => 'role',
    'team_subject_type' => 'team',
],
```

`teams` falls back to this key **only** when the host's own `config('permission.teams')`
is unset — the host's Spatie config is authoritative. `role_subject_type` /
`team_subject_type` are the morph aliases that role/team grant rows are addressed to.

### The team-switch and the cache seam

The full v8 dance — capture the current team id, `setPermissionsTeamId($workspaceId)`,
check, restore in a `finally` — lives entirely inside the driver, so concurrent panels
never bleed into each other. After the host mutates an actor's roles/permissions
**outside** Spatie's own assign/remove helpers, it must reset the cache so a stale,
team-scoped permission can't grant a revoked level on the next resolve:

```php
use Vaulter\Access\Drivers\SpatiePermissionDriver;

SpatiePermissionDriver::forgetCachedPermissions($actor);
```

This is a no-op when Spatie is not installed.

## AzGuard — the per-resource seam

`Vaulter\Azgard\AzgardPermissionDriver` lives in the separate
`axioma-studio/vaulter-azgard` package; core does not depend on AzGuard/Corex.

```bash
composer require axioma-studio/vaulter-azgard
```

Its Laravel-discovered provider registers `azgard` in `vaulter.permission_drivers`,
preserving an explicit host override, and binds
`Vaulter\Azgard\Contracts\AzgardGuard` to the real adapter. Then select
`VAULTER_PERMISSION_DRIVER=azgard`. Without the installed bridge, the key is unknown
and throws `MissingPermissionDriverException`.

The composite resolution order is node-ACL → workspace-scoped role → global. This driver
owns the **workspace-scoped role** lane:

- **`override`** = `isSuperAdmin()` → `Effect::Allow`, else `null` (never a deny).
- **`resolve`** maps each ranked level's defining ability to an AzGuard permission and
  asks `hasPermissionIn($workspaceType, $workspaceId, $permission)`; the highest allowed
  level becomes the `Decision`. (`AccessScope` is node-blind, so this is the
  workspace-scoped check.)
- **`subjectsFor`** = `[Subject(actor)]` only — AzGuard *answers* checks rather than
  enumerating role-subjects. A host that addresses grant rows to AzGuard roles should
  subclass and append those Subjects.
- **`canCreateInWorkspace`** asks `hasPermissionIn($type, $id, $createPermission)`.

The level → defining-ability probes are: `Reader → View`, `Commenter → Comment`,
`Writer → Edit`, `Organizer → Delete`, `Owner → Manage`.

### Configuration

Unlike Gate/Spatie (keyed by `GrantLevel`), the AzGuard map is **action-centric** —
keyed by `Ability`:

```php
// config/vaulter-azgard.php — used only when drivers.permission = 'azgard'
return [
    'panel_id' => null, // null resolves the panel from the permission key
    'permissions' => [
        'view'     => 'documents.view',
        'download' => 'documents.download',
        'comment'  => 'documents.comment',
        'edit'     => 'documents.update',
        'create'   => 'documents.create',
        'move'     => 'documents.update',
        'copy'     => 'documents.update',
        'trash'    => 'documents.delete',
        'delete'   => 'documents.delete',
        'restore'  => 'documents.delete',
        'share'    => 'documents.manage',
        'manage'   => 'documents.manage',
    ],
    'create_permission' => env('VAULTER_AZGARD_CREATE_PERMISSION', 'documents.create'),
];
```

### The AzgardGuard adapter

`Vaulter\Azgard\Contracts\AzgardGuard` is the narrow seam the driver talks to. It
exposes exactly the three checks the driver needs — and nothing of AzGuard's own API:

```php
interface AzgardGuard
{
    // Per-resource scoped permission (the per-node lane).
    public function hasScopedPermission(string $permission, object $entity): bool;

    // Workspace-scoped permission (the lane resolve()/create actually drive).
    public function hasPermissionIn(string $contextType, int|string $contextId, string $permission): bool;

    // The global SuperAdmin wildcard.
    public function isSuperAdmin(): bool;
}
```

If the actor itself implements `AzgardGuard`, the driver uses it directly.
Otherwise the bridge provider supplies `AzgardGuardAdapter` for the current user
implementing `Vaulter\Azgard\Contracts\AzgardBackedUser`. For guests or other users,
it returns `NullAzgardGuard`, which grants no permissions. The host must add
`AzgardBackedUser` to its user model and align the morph types.

::: details Optionally overriding the supplied adapter
The bridge already binds a real adapter. A host can override `AzgardGuard`, delegating to AzGuard's
`hasScopedPermission` / Corex `ContextGuard` `hasPermissionIn` and the SuperAdmin
wildcard. The method shapes mirror AzGuard 1:1, so the adapter is a thin pass-through:

```php
// In a host service provider
$this->app->bind(\Vaulter\Azgard\Contracts\AzgardGuard::class, function ($app) {
    $actor = $app['auth']->user();

    return new class ($actor) implements \Vaulter\Azgard\Contracts\AzgardGuard {
        public function __construct(private object $actor) {}

        public function hasScopedPermission(string $permission, object $entity): bool
        {
            return $this->actor->hasScopedPermission($permission, $entity);
        }

        public function hasPermissionIn(string $contextType, int|string $contextId, string $permission): bool
        {
            return $this->actor->hasPermissionIn($contextType, $contextId, $permission);
        }

        public function isSuperAdmin(): bool
        {
            return $this->actor->isSuperAdmin();
        }
    };
});
```

**Morph alignment (host responsibility):** the workspace/owner morph types must be
registered Corex morph aliases aligned with `vaulter.ids.default=ulid` +
`corex.ids.strategy=Ulid` + `AZ_GUARD_MORPH_TYPE=ulid`. The driver passes the workspace
type string through untouched — it never resolves the alias itself.
:::

### Testing the AzGuard lane

`Vaulter\Azgard\Testing\FakeAzgardGuard` is an in-memory guard supplied by
`vaulter-azgard`. Install the bridge and its Composer dependencies even for fake-based
tests; the fake replaces live AzGuard checks, not the package's installation requirements.

```php
use Vaulter\Azgard\Testing\FakeAzgardGuard;

// grant one workspace permission
app()->bind(\Vaulter\Azgard\Contracts\AzgardGuard::class,
    fn () => FakeAzgardGuard::grantingWorkspace('team', $teamId, 'documents.update'));

// or a super-admin
app()->bind(\Vaulter\Azgard\Contracts\AzgardGuard::class,
    fn () => FakeAzgardGuard::superAdmin());
```

## Driver comparison

| | Database | Gate | Spatie | AzGuard |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Extra dependency | none | none (built-in) | optional `spatie/laravel-permission` | `axioma-studio/vaulter-azgard` + its dependencies |
| Map keyed by | — | `GrantLevel` | `GrantLevel` | `Ability` |
| Enumerates role/team subjects | subclass | no | yes | no |
| Super-admin override | no | `vaulter.super` ability | super permission | SuperAdmin wildcard |
| Workspace-scoped | per-node grants | node-blind context | team-scoped | `hasPermissionIn` |
| Safe when not configured | n/a | yes | yes (deny) | only with the bridge installed |

- [Authorization](./authorization) — how a driver's answers are folded into the final
  decision.
- [Grants](./grants) — the `v_node_grants` rows the subject-set is matched against.
- [Multi-tenancy recipe](../guide/recipes) — end-to-end tenant + role wiring.
- ADR-0002 (authorization delegation), ADR-0007 (the AzGuard seam).

# Recipes

Practical, end-to-end recipes for the common ways teams embed Vaulter. Each one is grounded in
a real contract or config key — see [Architecture](/guide/architecture) for the mental model
and [Configuration](/guide/configuration) for every key in full.

[[toc]]

## Attach a Drive to a CRM task or project {#attach-drive}

The headline use case: give any host entity its own file/folder Drive with **zero migrations**.
`Vaulter::for($entity)` get-or-creates a `v_storages` row keyed by the polymorphic
`(owner_type, owner_id, panel)` triple and provisions a root folder — idempotent, so calling it
twice returns the same storage.

::: code-group

```php [Controller]
use Vaulter\Facades\Vaulter;

final class TaskDriveController
{
    public function index(\App\Models\Task $task)
    {
        // Authorize through your app, then open the Drive for this task.
        $drive = Vaulter::for($task);

        return response()->json([
            'storage' => $drive->model()->id,
            'nodes'   => $drive->list(), // Collection<Node> of the root's children
        ]);
    }

    public function store(\App\Models\Task $task, \Illuminate\Http\Request $request)
    {
        $drive = Vaulter::for($task);

        $node = $drive->upload(
            $request->file('document'),
            actorId: $request->user()->getKey(),
        );

        return response()->json(['node' => $node->id], 201);
    }
}
```

```vue [Vue]
<script setup lang="ts">
import { VaulterDrive } from '@vaulter/vue'

// The storage id resolved server-side (e.g. from Vaulter::for($task)->storage()->id).
const props = defineProps<{ storageId: string }>()
</script>

<template>
  <VaulterDrive :storage-id="props.storageId" />
</template>
```

:::

For a **dedicated** Drive on a specific entity type — with its own feature flags and a Filament
resource — define a Storage Profile instead of using the `default` panel:

```bash
php artisan vaulter:make:profile task_drive --host="App\\Models\\Task"
```

This scaffolds `app/Vaulter/Profiles/TaskDriveStoragePanel.php`. Edit its feature flags, then
register the provider FQCN in `config/vaulter.php`:

```php
// config/vaulter.php
'panels' => [
    \App\Vaulter\Profiles\TaskDriveStoragePanel::class,
],
```

```php
// app/Vaulter/Profiles/TaskDriveStoragePanel.php
use Vaulter\Profiles\Profile;
use Vaulter\Profiles\ProfileProvider;

final class TaskDriveStoragePanel extends ProfileProvider
{
    public function profile(Profile $panel): Profile
    {
        return $panel
            ->id('task_drive')
            ->host(\App\Models\Task::class)
            ->storageType('team')
            ->feature('document_versions', true) // enable in-app rich-text editing
            ->feature('share_links', true);      // enable bearer share links
    }
}
```

Now mount it with the panel id:

```php
$drive = Vaulter::for($task, panel: 'task_drive');
```

::: tip Zero migrations
A profile uses the shared `v_*` schema. `vaulter:make:profile` writes the provider;
register its FQCN in config. It creates no migration.
:::

## Multi-tenant SaaS storage {#multi-tenant}

Vaulter does **not** enforce tenancy — by design ([ADR-0003](/adr/0003-embeddability-data-model)).
The host owns the tenant boundary; Vaulter gives you the seams to express it. There are three
moving parts.

### 1. Add the tenant column

```php
// config/vaulter.php
'tenant' => [
    'enabled' => true,        // VAULTER_TENANT_ENABLED — adds a tenant_id column to the schema
    'column'  => 'tenant_id',
],
```

### 2. Supply a tenant-aware model

Vaulter resolves every model through `config('vaulter.models.*')`. Point one (or all) at your
own subclass that applies your tenant scope — Vaulter never scopes by `tenant_id` itself:

```php
// app/Models/Vaulter/Node.php
namespace App\Models\Vaulter;

use Vaulter\Models\Drive\Node as BaseNode;
use App\Models\Concerns\BelongsToTenant; // your existing global-scope trait

final class Node extends BaseNode
{
    use BelongsToTenant;
}
```

```php
// config/vaulter.php
'models' => [
    // ...
    'node'    => \App\Models\Vaulter\Node::class,
    'storage' => \App\Models\Vaulter\Storage::class,
],
```

### 3. Align dedup scope and ids

Per-tenant dedup is already the default, so a global dedup namespace can't leak the
*existence* of a file across tenants ([ADR-0012](/adr/0012-dedup-scope)):

```php
// config/vaulter.php
'dedup' => ['scope' => 'tenant'], // the default; never use 'global' for untrusted tenants
'ids'   => ['default' => 'ulid'], // ULID aligns with CoreX / AzGuard morph keys (ADR-0011)
```

::: warning Tenant scope is the host's responsibility
If you set `dedup.scope = 'global'` with multiple tenants you accept a cross-tenant existence
side channel. Keep it `tenant` (or `storage`) unless the tenants trust one another. If you swap
in a tenant-aware model, that model — not Vaulter — must apply the scope on *every* query.
:::

## Write a custom permission driver {#permission-driver}

The Drive ACL combines `v_node_grants` with a swappable `PermissionDriver` lane. To bridge your
app's role system, implement
[`Vaulter\Contracts\Access\PermissionDriver`](/guide/architecture#authorization). It is
**node-blind**: it never receives a `Node` — only an `Authorizable` actor and an `AccessScope`
(panel + workspace coordinates + node owner).

The simplest real driver subclasses the standalone `database` lane and just expands the
subject-set with the actor's roles/teams (so `v_node_grants` rows addressed to a role apply):

```php
namespace App\Vaulter;

use Vaulter\Access\Drivers\DatabasePermissionDriver;
use Vaulter\Access\ValueObjects\Subject;
use Illuminate\Contracts\Auth\Access\Authorizable;

final class TeamRoleDriver extends DatabasePermissionDriver
{
    /** @return list<Subject> */
    public function subjectsFor(Authorizable $actor): array
    {
        $subjects = parent::subjectsFor($actor); // [Subject(actor)]

        foreach ($actor->teams as $team) {
            $subjects[] = new Subject(type: 'team', id: $team->getKey());
        }

        return $subjects;
    }
}
```

A fuller driver also answers the role lane and the super-admin override:

```php
use Vaulter\Contracts\Access\PermissionDriver;
use Vaulter\Access\ValueObjects\AccessScope;
use Vaulter\Access\ValueObjects\Decision;
use Vaulter\Access\ValueObjects\Subject;
use Vaulter\Enums\Access\Effect;
use Vaulter\Enums\Access\GrantLevel;

final class AppRoleDriver implements PermissionDriver
{
    public function override(Authorizable $actor, AccessScope $scope): ?Effect
    {
        return $actor->is_super_admin ? Effect::Allow : null; // absolute, step 1
    }

    public function resolve(Subject $subject, Authorizable $actor, AccessScope $scope): ?Decision
    {
        // Raise access from a host role — folded as roleAllow into max(aclAllow, roleAllow).
        // It can RAISE access but never override a deny (the final veto still applies).
        if ($actor->canEditIn($scope->workspaceType, $scope->workspaceId)) {
            // Decision::allow(level) defaults bits to the level's bitmask;
            // pass explicit bits only to narrow them.
            return Decision::allow(GrantLevel::Writer);
        }

        return null; // nothing to say — the ACL is the sole authority
    }

    /** @return list<Subject> */
    public function subjectsFor(Authorizable $actor): array
    {
        return [Subject::ofModel($actor)];
    }

    public function canCreateInWorkspace(Authorizable $actor, string $workspaceType, int|string $workspaceId): bool
    {
        return $actor->canCreateIn($workspaceType, $workspaceId);
    }
}
```

Register it as a named driver and select it:

```php
// config/vaulter.php
'drivers' => [
    'permission' => env('VAULTER_PERMISSION_DRIVER', 'app'),
],

'permission_drivers' => [
    'database' => \Vaulter\Access\Drivers\DatabasePermissionDriver::class,
    'gate'     => \Vaulter\Access\Drivers\GatePermissionDriver::class,
    'spatie'   => \Vaulter\Access\Drivers\SpatiePermissionDriver::class,
    'app'      => \App\Vaulter\AppRoleDriver::class, // your driver
],
```

::: tip Use a shipped lane first
For Laravel Gate, Spatie Permission v8, or AzGuard you do **not** need a custom class — set
`drivers.permission` to `gate` / `spatie` / `azgard` and fill the matching config block
(`vaulter.gate.*` / `vaulter.spatie.*` / `vaulter-azgard.*`). For AzGuard install
`composer require axioma-studio/vaulter-azgard`: its provider registers the driver
and adapter automatically. The user model must implement `AzgardBackedUser` — see
[Permission drivers](/guide/permission-drivers).
:::

## Write a custom format handler {#format-handler}

A `FileHandler` claims mime types / extensions and tells the client how to mount a node
(editor, preview, or download). The core-owned `Vaulter\Handlers\FileHandlerRegistry` resolves
the best one by mime → extension → capability → priority, falling back to the `DownloadOnlyHandler`.
Adding a
format is **one class + one register call — no migration, no core change**
([H.5 / ADR-0004](/adr/0004-content-format)).

```php
namespace App\Vaulter\Handlers;

use Vaulter\Contracts\Handlers\FileHandler;
use Vaulter\ValueObjects\Handlers\FileDescriptor;
use Vaulter\ValueObjects\Handlers\ContentCapabilities;
use Vaulter\ValueObjects\Handlers\ViewerDescriptor;

final class CadHandler implements FileHandler
{
    public function key(): string { return 'acme/cad'; }

    /** @return list<string> */
    public function mimeTypes(): array { return ['application/acad', 'image/vnd.dwg']; }

    /** @return list<string> */
    public function extensions(): array { return ['dwg', 'dxf']; }

    // Higher wins among handlers matching the same file; DownloadOnly sits lowest.
    public function priority(): int { return 100; }

    public function capabilities(FileDescriptor $file): ContentCapabilities
    {
        return new ContentCapabilities(
            editable: false,
            previewable: true,
            downloadable: true,
            thumbnailable: true,
            collaborative: false,
        );
    }

    public function viewer(FileDescriptor $file): ViewerDescriptor
    {
        // The viewer key + props the client routes the node to.
        return new ViewerDescriptor(
            key: 'acme/cad',
            props: ['mime' => $file->canonicalMime()],
        );
    }
}
```

Register it any of three ways — config FQCN (cache-safe), a runtime call, or a tagged binding:

::: code-group

```php [config]
// config/vaulter.php
'handlers' => [
    \Vaulter\Documents\Engines\Handlers\TipTapHandler::class,
    \App\Vaulter\Handlers\CadHandler::class, // before the fallbacks
    \Vaulter\Handlers\Builtin\PreviewHandler::class,
    \Vaulter\Handlers\Builtin\DownloadOnlyHandler::class,
],
```

```php [runtime]
// A service provider's boot()
use Vaulter\Facades\Vaulter;

Vaulter::handlers()->register(\App\Vaulter\Handlers\CadHandler::class);
```

```php [tagged]
// A service provider's register()
$this->app->tag([\App\Vaulter\Handlers\CadHandler::class], 'vaulter.file_handlers');
```

:::

::: details Confirm the descriptor that ships to the client
`GET nodes/{node}/handler` returns the resolved handler's `id`, capabilities and `ViewerDescriptor`
for a node — exactly what the Vue client reads to pick an editor/preview implementation. (This
route is gated on the `document_versions` feature.)
:::

## Swap the storage disk to S3 {#s3-disk}

Vaulter's byte plane is a content-addressed store over a Flysystem disk. To use S3 you usually
only change config — no custom class needed.

### Point Vaulter at an S3 disk

```php
// config/filesystems.php — a standard Laravel S3 disk
'disks' => [
    's3-vaulter' => [
        'driver' => 's3',
        'key'    => env('AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID'),
        'secret' => env('AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY'),
        'region' => env('AWS_DEFAULT_REGION'),
        'bucket' => env('VAULTER_S3_BUCKET'),
    ],
],
```

```dotenv
# .env
VAULTER_DISK=s3-vaulter
```

`config('vaulter.storage.default_disk')` is the canonical CAS disk used when a storage row does
not pin its own `disk`. The shipped `FlysystemStorageDriver` already does the right thing on S3:
a conditional create (`If-None-Match: *`), short-lived signed URLs via `temporaryUrl`, and the
scope-qualified key layout.

::: danger Never version the CAS bucket
The CAS bucket must be **unversioned**. Do **not** use S3 lifecycle/versioning as a
blob-deletion mechanism — Vaulter owns deletion through its two-phase GC. The only S3 lifecycle
rule you should add is `AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload` as a backstop for abandoned resumable
uploads ([ADR-0006](/adr/0006-content-addressed-blobs-gc)).
:::

### Swap a CAS service for object-store specifics

If you need behaviour the default driver doesn't cover, implement
`Vaulter\Contracts\Cas\StorageDriver` (or `ContentStore` / `BlobStore`) and bind it:

```php
// config/vaulter.php
'cas' => [
    'content_store'  => \Vaulter\Media\Cas\Sha256ContentStore::class,
    'storage_driver' => \App\Vaulter\S3ChecksumDriver::class, // your driver
    'blob_store'     => \Vaulter\Media\Cas\BlobStore::class,
],
```

The `StorageDriver` surface: `disk()`, `put($key, $stream, $disk, $ifNoneMatch, $options)`,
`get()`, `exists()`, `delete()`, `temporaryUrl($key, $expiresAt, $disk)`.

## Custom export format {#custom-export}

The built-in `html` and `markdown` exporters render a document's TipTap content. Add your own
(PDF, DOCX, …) by implementing `Vaulter\Contracts\Handlers\DocumentExporter`:

```php
namespace App\Vaulter;

use Vaulter\Contracts\Handlers\DocumentContent;
use Vaulter\Contracts\Handlers\DocumentExporter;
use Vaulter\Exceptions\Documents\UnsupportedDocumentContentException;
use Vaulter\Documents\ValueObjects\TipTapContent;

final class PdfExporter implements DocumentExporter
{
    public function format(): string { return 'pdf'; }
    public function mimeType(): string { return 'application/pdf'; }
    public function extension(): string { return 'pdf'; }

    public function export(DocumentContent $content): string
    {
        // The contract is opaque — narrow to what this exporter understands.
        if (!$content instanceof TipTapContent) {
            throw UnsupportedDocumentContentException::forExporter(
                $this->format(), TipTapContent::class, $content::class,
            );
        }

        // Binary formats return an encoded string (e.g. base64) + the matching mime.
        return MyPdfLibrary::fromTiptap($content->toArray())->toBytes();
    }
}
```

Register it via config or at runtime:

::: code-group

```php [config]
// config/vaulter.php
'exporters' => [
    'html'     => \Vaulter\Export\HtmlExporter::class,
    'markdown' => \Vaulter\Export\MarkdownExporter::class,
    'pdf'      => \App\Vaulter\PdfExporter::class,
],
```

```php [runtime]
use Vaulter\Facades\Vaulter;

Vaulter::registerExporter(new \App\Vaulter\PdfExporter());
```

:::

It is then reachable at `GET nodes/{node}/export?format=pdf` and via the Vue
`useDocumentNode(nodeId).exportAs('pdf')` composable.

## Custom share-token shape {#share-token}

By default share tokens are random strings. To mint short, hashed, or prefixed tokens, implement
`Vaulter\Contracts\Sharing\ShareTokenGenerator` (a token must be unique and fit the token
column, ≤ 64 chars):

```php
namespace App\Vaulter;

use Vaulter\Contracts\Sharing\ShareTokenGenerator;

final class ShortTokenGenerator implements ShareTokenGenerator
{
    public function generate(): string
    {
        return \Illuminate\Support\Str::lower(\Illuminate\Support\Str::random(12));
    }
}
```

```php
// config/vaulter.php
'share' => [
    'token_generator' => \App\Vaulter\ShortTokenGenerator::class,
    'url_base'        => env('VAULTER_SHARE_URL_BASE', '/share'),
    'prefix_length'   => 8,
],
```

::: info Hash-only storage
Only the `sha256` of the token is ever stored (`token_hash`), with a short `token_prefix` for
owner-side lookup. The raw token is returned to the creator exactly once and never re-exposed
([ADR-0013](/adr/0013-two-sharing-channels)).
:::

## Blob garbage collection on a schedule {#blob-gc}

Trashing or replacing files leaves blobs unreferenced. The two-phase GC tombstones them, then
sweeps after a grace window; a separate reconcile job repairs `ref_count` drift.

```php
// routes/console.php (Laravel 11+) or app/Console/Kernel.php
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Schedule;

// Trash retention → permanently force-deletes nodes past trash.retention_days.
Schedule::command('vaulter:purge-trash')->daily();

// Two-phase blob GC: tombstone unreferenced blobs, sweep tombstoned past grace.
Schedule::command('vaulter:blobs:gc')->hourly();

// Repair ref_count drift + flag dangling rows (run less often, off-peak).
// Add --orphans to ALSO disk-walk for orphan objects (report-only; see Storage & Blobs).
Schedule::command('vaulter:blobs:reconcile')->dailyAt('03:00');

// Reclaim resumable-upload sessions older than uploads.session_ttl_hours.
Schedule::command('vaulter:sweep-uploads')->hourly();
```

The grace window is `config('vaulter.gc.grace_hours')` (default 24, floored at 1h). It **must**
be ≥ your worst-case multipart-commit latency so an in-flight upload can resurrect a tombstoned
blob first.

```bash
# Override the grace window ad hoc, and also clear crashed-staging PENDING rows.
php artisan vaulter:blobs:gc --grace=48 --pending
```

::: danger --pending sweeps crashed uploads
`--pending` sweeps `PENDING` blobs left by a crashed staging step. Run it only when you are
sure no upload is mid-flight, or keep the grace window generous — a too-short grace can sweep a
blob a slow multipart commit was about to reference.
:::

## Reliability — outbox & webhooks {#webhooks}

The `reliability` feature stages each Drive domain event in `v_outbox` (after-commit), then a
relay fans it out into signed `v_webhook_deliveries` rows per active subscribed endpoint:

```php
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Schedule;

Schedule::command('vaulter:relay-outbox')->everyMinute();    // outbox → deliveries → queue
Schedule::command('vaulter:retry-webhooks')->everyFiveMinutes(); // retry failed deliveries
Schedule::command('vaulter:prune-webhooks')->daily();        // reclaim settled audit history
```

Subscriber endpoints are managed through the `webhook-endpoints` routes (gated by the
`WebhookEndpointPolicy` manage ability). Each delivery POST carries an HMAC-SHA256 signature
(`X-Vaulter-Signature`), a timestamp (`X-Vaulter-Timestamp`) and the event name
(`X-Vaulter-Event`); consumers **dedupe on the `event_id`** in the payload, since delivery is
at-least-once. Tune `config('vaulter.webhooks.*')` (`max_attempts`, `backoff`,
`disable_after_failures`).

### Pruning settled outbox & webhook history

The relayed outbox rows and terminal webhook deliveries are an append-only audit trail that
otherwise grows forever. `vaulter:prune-webhooks` reclaims the **settled** rows past a
retention window — and *only* the settled ones:

```bash
# Prune settled rows older than config('vaulter.webhooks.retention_days') (default 30):
php artisan vaulter:prune-webhooks

# Override the window, or preview the exact counts without deleting anything:
php artisan vaulter:prune-webhooks --days=7
php artisan vaulter:prune-webhooks --dry-run
```

It deletes exactly two kinds of row that never change again:

- **dispatched outbox rows** — status `dispatched`, by `dispatched_at`;
- **terminal deliveries** — status `delivered` or `dead` (DLQ), by `updated_at` (the
  terminalisation time).

In-flight rows are **never** touched: a `pending` outbox row (the relay still owns it) and a
`pending`/`failed` delivery (the due-retry sweep still owns it) are left alone regardless of
age. `--dry-run` reports the counts it *would* remove without deleting a row. The command is
gated on the `reliability` feature — with the feature off it no-ops with a notice (the
`v_outbox` / `v_webhook_*` tables may not exist). The retention default lives at
`config('vaulter.webhooks.retention_days')` (30, floored at 0). Schedule it alongside the
relay/retry commands above.

## Testing with the shipped doubles {#testing}

Vaulter ships test doubles under `Vaulter\Testing\*` so a consumer can boot without wiring a
real role system:

- **`NullPermissionDriver`** — an open driver (every actor is a super-admin) for tests / local dev.
  It is rejected in production, so it can never silently open a prod install.
- **`Vaulter\Azgard\Testing\FakeAzgardGuard`** — a guard double for the `azgard` lane;
  the bridge and its Composer dependencies must be installed.

```php
// In a Pest test, force the open driver for the duration of the test.
config()->set('vaulter.drivers.permission', 'null'); // non-production only

$drive = Vaulter::for($task);
$node  = $drive->upload('hello', name: 'note.txt');

expect($node->name)->toBe('note.txt');
```

---
title: Storage & Blobs
description: How Vaulter stores file bytes — content-addressed blobs keyed by sha256, per-scope deduplication, the race-free two-phase garbage collector, and Flysystem disks.
outline: deep
---

# Storage & Blobs

Vaulter never copies file bytes into its own tables. Every uploaded file is stored
**once** as an immutable, content-addressed **blob** on a Flysystem disk, and the
database keeps only metadata: the `sha256`, the size, the disk, the scope-qualified
key, a lifecycle status, and the edges that pin the blob to file versions.

This is the **content-addressed store (CAS)**. It gives you transparent
deduplication, a clear separation between *bytes on disk* and *rows in the
database*, and a garbage collector that is safe to run while uploads are in flight.

::: info Where this lives
The CAS implementation is in `Vaulter\Media\Cas\*` (package `axioma-studio/vaulter-media`;
the host-facing `BlobLock` stays at `Vaulter\Cas\BlobLock` in core), the row model is
`Vaulter\Models\Cas\Blob`, the lifecycle enum is `Vaulter\Enums\Cas\BlobStatus`, and
configuration sits under the `cas`, `dedup`, `gc` and `storage` keys of
`config/vaulter.php`.
:::

## The mental model

```
upload stream
     │
     ▼
ContentStore::stage()   ─► local seekable temp file, sha256 recomputed from THOSE bytes
     │
     ▼
BlobStore::commitStaged() ─► one locked transaction: find-or-create v_blobs row by (scope_key, sha256)
     │                       └─ dedup hit?  reuse the row, skip the physical write
     ▼
ContentStore::promote() ─► write staged bytes to "<scope>/ab/<sha256>" on the disk
     │
     ▼
v_file_version_blobs    ─► the EDGE that pins the blob alive (liveness truth)
```

Three contracts split the work, and all three are swappable through `config('vaulter.cas')`:

| Contract | Default | Responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| `Vaulter\Contracts\Cas\BlobStore` | `Vaulter\Media\Cas\BlobStore` | High-level lifecycle: `commit` / `commitStaged` / `attach` / `detach` / `read`. Prepared and stream CAS entry points. |
| `Vaulter\Contracts\Cas\ContentStore` | `Vaulter\Media\Cas\Sha256ContentStore` | Byte side: `stage` / `promote` / `get` / `exists` / `delete` / `keyFor`. Knows bytes, hashes and keys — never a `v_blobs` row. |
| `Vaulter\Contracts\Cas\StorageDriver` | `Vaulter\Media\Cas\FlysystemStorageDriver` | Thin Flysystem abstraction: `put` / `get` / `exists` / `delete` / `temporaryUrl` / `disk`. |

```php
// config/vaulter.php
'cas' => [
    'content_store'  => \Vaulter\Media\Cas\Sha256ContentStore::class,
    'storage_driver' => \Vaulter\Media\Cas\FlysystemStorageDriver::class,
    'blob_store'     => \Vaulter\Media\Cas\BlobStore::class,
],
```

All three are bound in the service provider and resolved through the container, so
the values are config-cache safe (FQCNs only, no closures). Point any of them at
your own class to change how bytes are staged, hashed, promoted, or stored — see
[Recipes › Custom storage driver](/guide/recipes).

## Bytes on disk, metadata in the database

A blob is just metadata. The `v_blobs` row (model `Vaulter\Models\Cas\Blob`) carries:

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `sha256` | The lowercase hex content address (always recomputed server-side). |
| `size_bytes` | Authoritative size of the durable bytes. |
| `disk` | The Flysystem disk the canonical object lives on. |
| `storage_key` | The scope-qualified path of the object — `"<scope>/ab/<sha256>"`. |
| `status` | Lifecycle state (see [Blob lifecycle](#blob-lifecycle)). |
| `ref_count` | A **reconciled cache** of the live edge count — *not* the liveness truth. |
| `dedup_scope` | `global` \| `tenant` \| `storage` — the boundary the address is unique within. |
| `scope_key` | Lossless `global`, `tenant:{id}` or `drive:{id}`; unique together with `sha256`. |
| `tenant_id` / `storage_id` | Informational scope IDs; `scope_key` owns deduplication. |
| `first_seen_at` / `committed_at` / `delete_after_at` | Staging, commit, and GC-grace timestamps. |

The bytes themselves never appear in any column. The model timestamps are disabled
(`public $timestamps = false`) — the CAS manages its own three timestamps.

### The storage key is scope-qualified

`ContentStore::keyFor(BlobScope $scope, string $sha256)` uses the first two digest
characters as one shard: `{scope-segment}/{sha[0:2]}/{sha}`. Historical scopes keep
`{legacy-segment}/{sha[0:2]}/{sha[2:4]}/{sha}`. Migration preserves their stored paths;
reads always use the blob row's `storage_key` and `disk`.

::: warning Why the scope segment matters
Under per-scope dedup, two scopes may legitimately hold the same `sha256`. Without
the scope segment baked into the key, *one* scope's garbage collector could delete
*another* scope's live bytes. The scope segment guarantees distinct scopes never
resolve to the same physical object.
:::

The scope segment is derived from the dedup scope:

- `global` → `g`
- `tenant` → `t-{id}`, or `g` when there is no tenant
- `storage` → `d-{id}`

`BlobScope` preserves string IDs, including UUIDs, ULIDs and leading zeroes.
Identifiers contain 1–96 bytes. An ID matching `[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}` is used verbatim;
other IDs use `~` followed by unpadded base64url. `fromSegment()` reverses this
encoding and rejects noncanonical segments. Legacy factories retain `global`,
`s<id>`, `t<id>`, `snull` and `tnull` paths.

## Hashing: the staged file, never the live stream

`Sha256ContentStore::stage()` drains the incoming stream into a **local, seekable
temp file** (in 1 MiB chunks) and computes the `sha256` from *those durable bytes*.

::: danger Vaulter never trusts a client-supplied hash
The content address is **always** recomputed server-side from the staged file — a
lying client `sha256`, a resumable-upload `expected_sha256`, or an S3 multipart
`ETag` are never used as the content address. Hashing happens *outside* the database
transaction, so hashing a multi-GB upload never holds the row/advisory lock.
:::

The staged object (`Vaulter\Media\Cas\StagedTempObject`, implementing
`Vaulter\Contracts\Cas\StagedObject`) exposes `path()`, `sha256()`, `sizeBytes()`,
`readStream()` and an idempotent `discard()` that removes the temp file once the
bytes are promoted (or the commit rolls back).

## Deduplication & `dedup.scope`

The dedup scope decides the boundary a content address is unique within:

```php
// config/vaulter.php
'dedup' => [
    'scope' => env('VAULTER_DEDUP_SCOPE', 'tenant'), // global|tenant|storage
],
```

| Scope | Uniqueness | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `global` | `UNIQUE (scope_key, sha256)` | One physical object per `sha256` across the whole install. |
| `tenant` | `UNIQUE (scope_key, sha256)` | One object per tenant — no cross-tenant existence leak. **Default.** |
| `storage` | `UNIQUE (scope_key, sha256)` | One object per storage container. |

`BlobScope::forUpload()` selects a `scope_key` from this setting. The schema always
uses `UNIQUE(scope_key, sha256)`; scope changes do not alter that index shape.
`UNIQUE(storage_key)` remains an independent physical-address guard.

::: tip The UNIQUE index is the portable race backbone
When two requests upload identical bytes concurrently, the `UNIQUE (scope_key, sha256)`
constraint is the cross-database backbone: one `INSERT` wins, the loser catches the
unique violation, re-`SELECT`s the winning row, and reuses it. This holds on
PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite even where the advisory lock below is a no-op.
:::

::: warning Choosing a scope is a one-way door
The scope is stored in every blob's `scope_key` and `storage_key`. Pick
it at install time. `tenant` is the safe default for multi-tenant apps because it
prevents one tenant from learning another tenant holds a given file (an existence
leak), at the cost of storing identical bytes once per tenant. See
[Multi-tenancy](/guide/multi-tenancy) for how `dedup.scope = tenant` interacts with
host-owned tenancy.
:::

## The commit flow

`BlobStore::commit()` is the single CAS entry point. It runs **one** transaction
whose **first statement** is the per-`(scope, sha256)` lock, so every liveness
decision is made from rows read *after* the lock:

```php
// Vaulter\Media\Cas\BlobStore::commit() — simplified
$staged = $this->content->stage($stream);          // 1. stage + hash OUTSIDE the tx
$key    = $this->content->keyFor($scope, $staged->sha256());

$this->database->transaction(function () use (…) {
    $this->database->advisoryLock('cas:'.$scope->key().':'.$staged->sha256());          // 2. lock = statement #1

    $result = $this->blobs->findOrCreate(…);                  // 3. find-or-create by dedup key
                                                              //    (a tombstoned match is RESURRECTED)

    if ($result['created'] || !$this->content->exists($key)) { // 4. promote bytes only when needed
        $this->content->promote($staged, $key, $disk);
    }

    return $result['blob'];
});
```

Key properties (all from `Vaulter\Media\Cas\BlobStore`):

- **Staging happens outside the transaction.** Only the liveness decision is locked.
- **A dedup hit skips the physical write.** Bytes are promoted only when the row is
  newly created (or the canonical object is somehow missing — `promote()` is
  idempotent and conditional, so a resurrected row whose object vanished is
  re-promoted safely).
- **No synchronous `ref_count++`.** The liveness truth is the *edge* in
  `v_file_version_blobs`; `ref_count` is a reconciled cache that may lag.

### Attaching and reading

A committed blob is pinned alive by a **version↔blob edge**:

```php
$blobStore->attach($fileVersion, $blob, ['role' => 'data', 'ordinal' => 0]);
$blobStore->detach($fileVersion, $blob);   // bytes are NOT deleted here — GC handles that
$stream = $blobStore->read($blob);         // resource|null over the canonical bytes
```

In the Drive, `IngestFileAction` prepares and hashes bytes through
`ContentStore::stage()` before entering its SQL transaction. Inside the transaction,
locks follow **drive → nodes by id → file aggregate → quota → CAS**. A revision
reads its previous head and `version_count` from the locked file; its new number is
`version_count + 1` and its quota delta is new size minus that head's size.

`DriveStoreRepository::reserveBytes()` applies a conditional atomic UPDATE:
`used_bytes = used_bytes + delta` only when the quota is unlimited or the result
fits `quota_bytes`. A failed reservation throws `QuotaExceededException` and rolls
back all metadata. Copies reserve the sum of their subtree's heads in one UPDATE.
`used_bytes` includes heads in the trash; only purge frees those bytes.

The upload then calls `BlobStore::commitStaged($staged, $scope, $disk)`, creates the
file/version/edge and updates the head. `commitStaged()` leaves the staged object
intact. Its caller discards it in `finally`, after completion or failure, so SQL
serialization/deadlock retries (up to three attempts) reuse the same prepared bytes.
`commit($stream, $scope, $disk)` remains the convenience stage/commitStaged/discard
entry point. Custom `BlobStore` implementations must implement `commitStaged()`.

Promotion is an idempotent storage operation outside SQL rollback: **stage →
promote → metadata commit**. A failure after promotion can leave canonical bytes
without a blob row. Reconciliation collects these orphans after the configured
grace period under the same CAS lock, preserving objects referenced by winners.

## Blob lifecycle

`Vaulter\Enums\Cas\BlobStatus` is the state machine:

```
Pending → Committed → Tombstoned → Deleting → Deleted
              ↑____________|
             (resurrection)
```

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Pending` | Row exists, bytes staged but not yet durable+verified. A crashed staging leaves a `Pending` row swept on timeout. |
| `Committed` | Bytes durable, `sha256` verified — the live state. |
| `Tombstoned` | GC marked it unreferenced; `delete_after_at` carries the grace deadline. A concurrent commit **resurrects** it back to `Committed`. |
| `Deleting` | The sweep claimed it; the physical delete is in flight. |
| `Deleted` | Bytes gone; the row is kept as an idempotent tombstone so a re-run of the sweep is a no-op. |

The enum enforces legal transitions via `allowedTransitions()` / `canTransitionTo()`,
and `isLive()` returns true for `Pending` and `Committed` (both pin their bytes).

## Garbage collection (two-phase, race-free)

When you trash and purge a file, its version edges detach. A blob with no remaining
edges is *garbage* — but deleting its bytes safely, while uploads may be
resurrecting that exact `sha256`, is the hard part. Vaulter's GC
(`Vaulter\Media\Cas\BlobGarbageCollector`) solves it in two phases, **ACL-blind** and run
as the system (a node a user cannot see still pins its blob).

### Phase 1 — mark

Scan `committed ∧ ref_count <= 0` (the `scopeGarbageCollectable` query). For each
candidate, under the per-`(scope, sha256)` lock, **re-verify** that:

- the status is still `Committed` (the cheap scan may be stale), and
- no live edge exists in `v_file_version_blobs`.

If both hold, `tombstone()` sets `status = Tombstoned` and `delete_after_at = now +
grace`. The grace deadline is armed *here*, so the sweep can never delete within the
grace window.

### Phase 2 — sweep

Take `tombstoned` blobs past their grace (`scopeSweepable`). Under the lock,
re-verify the blob is still `Tombstoned`, still has no live edge, and is past
`delete_after_at`. Only then: `markDeleting` → physical delete of the
scope-qualified object → `markDeleted` (an idempotent tombstone; a missing object is
fine).

::: tip The safety invariant
Every transaction that changes a content address's liveness — upload-commit,
GC-mark, GC-sweep — takes the per-`(scope, sha256)` lock as its **first statement**
and decides from rows read *after* it. That is what makes online GC safe: a commit
that wins the lock resurrects a tombstoned blob *before* the sweep can see it; a
sweep that wins the lock re-checks edge existence *before* deleting.
:::

Per database driver (`Vaulter\Cas\BlobLock`):

- **PostgreSQL** — `pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext(scope||sha256))`, a real mutex
  held for the whole transaction. The sweep additionally runs `SERIALIZABLE` with
  retry-on-`40001` (up to 5 attempts).
- **MySQL / MariaDB** — no transaction-advisory lock that survives like PG's, so the
  store relies on `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` on the blob row; the advisory helper is a
  no-op.
- **SQLite** — single-writer; the transaction itself serialises.

The `UNIQUE (scope_key, sha256)` constraint is the portable backbone that holds on all
three even when the advisory lock is a no-op.

### Pending sweep

`sweepPending()` clears rows from a crashed staging — a `Pending` row older than the
grace window (`first_seen_at < now − grace`) that carries no edge. Its possibly
partial object is deleted and the row finalised as a deleted tombstone, under the
lock so a slow-but-live commit is never stolen.

### Running the collector

```bash
# Both phases (mark + sweep), grace from config('vaulter.gc.grace_hours'):
php artisan vaulter:blobs:gc

# Override the grace window (floored at 1h):
php artisan vaulter:blobs:gc --grace=48

# Also clear crashed-staging PENDING rows:
php artisan vaulter:blobs:gc --pending
```

The command prints a per-phase tally — `Tombstoned X, swept Y, skipped Z (grace Nh)`.

```php
// config/vaulter.php
'gc' => [
    'grace_hours'        => env('VAULTER_GC_GRACE_HOURS', 24),
    // The separate, generally more generous window for the orphan disk-walk
    // (see Reconciliation below). Defaults to gc.grace_hours, floored at 1h.
    'orphan_grace_hours' => env('VAULTER_ORPHAN_GRACE_HOURS', env('VAULTER_GC_GRACE_HOURS', 24)),
],
```

::: warning The grace window must outlast your slowest upload
A tombstoned blob can be resurrected by an in-flight upload of the same `sha256`. The
grace must be **≥ the worst-case multipart-commit latency** so an upload can
resurrect first. It is floored at 1h by `Config::gcGraceHours()` regardless of
config — never set it to zero expecting an immediate purge.
:::

::: details Schedule it yourself
`vaulter:blobs:gc` and `vaulter:blobs:reconcile` are registered by the package but
**not** auto-scheduled — Vaulter does not touch your scheduler. Add them where you
schedule maintenance, e.g. in `routes/console.php`:

```php
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Schedule;

Schedule::command('vaulter:blobs:reconcile')->daily();
Schedule::command('vaulter:blobs:gc --pending')->dailyAt('03:00');
```

Run reconcile *before* GC so `ref_count` reflects reality when the mark scan reads it.
:::

See [Recipes › Blob GC & reconcile cron](/guide/recipes) for a full operations
recipe.

## Reconciliation: rebuilding the `ref_count` cache

`ref_count` is a cache, not the truth, so it drifts. `vaulter:blobs:reconcile`
(backed by `Vaulter\Media\Cas\BlobReconciler`) rebuilds it from the
`v_file_version_blobs` edge counts — the real liveness source — and reports
integrity hazards. It **never deletes anything**.

```bash
php artisan vaulter:blobs:reconcile
```

It walks every blob, rewrites any stale `ref_count`, and flags **dangling rows** — a
`Committed` blob whose canonical object is *missing on disk* (a half-promoted commit
or a botched manual delete). The command exits non-zero and warns with the offending
blob keys:

```
Reconciled 1240 blobs, corrected 3 ref_count caches.
Dangling rows (committed blob, missing object): 01J…ABC, 01J…XYZ
```

### Orphan objects: the disk walk

A dangling row is one of two inverse integrity hazards; the other is the **orphan
object** — bytes on disk that match the committed CAS key layout but have **no blob
row at all** (a commit that promoted its bytes then rolled the row back, or leaked
bytes). Detecting it requires walking the *disk*, the inverse of the row-side
reconcile above. The `--orphans` flag adds that disk-walk to the same command:

```bash
# Detect orphan objects (report-only) in addition to the row-side reconcile:
php artisan vaulter:blobs:reconcile --orphans

# Scan a specific disk and override the orphan grace window (hours, floored at 1h):
php artisan vaulter:blobs:reconcile --orphans --disk=s3 --orphan-grace=48

# DELETE the orphans found — PostgreSQL/MySQL only (refused on SQLite; see below):
php artisan vaulter:blobs:reconcile --orphans --prune
```

It prints its own line next to the reconcile tally:

```
Orphan walk (report-only): scanned 1240, found 2, pruned 0, skipped 1238 (disk s3, grace 24h).
Orphan objects (bytes with no blob row): t42/ab/cd/abcd…ef, t42/12/34/1234…99
```

::: warning Report-only by default — and the run FAILS when it finds orphans
Without `--prune` the walk only **detects and reports** orphans (a safe dry run on
every driver). Like the dangling-row check, a report-only run that finds any orphan
**exits non-zero** so cron/CI sees the hazard. Only a `--prune` run that actually
deleted them exits success.
:::

The sweep is built to *only ever* touch genuine canonical orphans. Its guards, in
order:

1. **Exact CAS-key layout, round-trip verified.** A path is a candidate only when it
   exactly matches `"<scope>/<a>/<b>/<sha256>"` *and* `keyFor(scope, sha256)`
   re-derives the **same** path — so the shard bytes are the real shard of that
   digest. Staging/tmp parts, resumable-upload fragments, foreign files and any
   mis-sharded path never match and are **never** considered for deletion.
2. **Any blob row means owned.** A matching object that has *any* `v_blobs` row (any
   status, looked up disk-agnostically since `storage_key` is globally unique) is
   owned, not an orphan.
3. **The orphan-grace window.** A row-less object is a deletable orphan only once it
   is **older than the orphan grace** — a just-promoted object may be a
   commit-in-progress whose row is not yet durable. Anything younger than the grace
   (or whose age the disk can't report) is skipped, never deleted.
4. **Locked recheck before delete.** A `--prune` delete happens under the same
   per-`(scope, sha256)` lock the GC uses, re-checking both row-absence and the grace
   *after* taking the lock, then deletes idempotently — so a commit that just created
   the owning row can never have its bytes swept out from under it.

::: danger `--prune` is refused on SQLite — PostgreSQL/MySQL only
The prune deletes bytes under a **write-less** critical section, which only serialises
against a concurrent commit on a driver whose lock orders a no-row-write section
(PostgreSQL advisory xact lock; MySQL `FOR UPDATE`). On **SQLite** that ordering never
engages — a concurrent commit could insert the owning row between the recheck and the
delete — so pruning is **refused** there (the command warns and degrades to
report-only). **Detection works on every driver**; only the destructive `--prune`
requires PostgreSQL/MySQL. Run report-only locally, or prune against the production DB.
:::

::: info A disk that can't be enumerated is skipped, not failed
The disk-walk needs a CAS content store that can list the disk (a `ListableContentStore`).
If the active store does **not** implement it, the walk reports `"listing unsupported"`,
scans nothing, and exits cleanly. A listable store over a backend that returns no entries
(for example a non-`FilesystemAdapter` disk that can't be enumerated) simply scans **zero**
objects — equally safe: nothing is enumerated, so nothing is deleted. Either way the
row-side reconcile result still stands.
:::

::: details The orphan grace is separate from the GC grace
The orphan walk uses `config('vaulter.gc.orphan_grace_hours')`
(env `VAULTER_ORPHAN_GRACE_HOURS`), which **defaults to `gc.grace_hours`** (24) and is
floored at 1h. Keep it ≥ your worst-case multipart-commit latency for the same reason
the GC grace must be generous: an in-flight resumable upload can promote its bytes long
before its row commits, and a fresh object must never be mistaken for an orphan.
:::

## Flysystem disks: `local`, S3, and per-storage

Blobs live on a standard Laravel Flysystem disk. The disk for a given blob is
resolved per call by `FlysystemStorageDriver::disk()`: a blob's own `disk` column
(set from the owning `v_storages.disk`) wins, otherwise the install default:

```php
// config/vaulter.php
'storage' => [
    'default_disk' => env('VAULTER_DISK', 'local'),
],
```

Because it is just a Flysystem disk, any driver works — `local`, `s3`, or a custom
one — configured in your app's `config/filesystems.php`. The CAS only does stream
writes plus a few object-store niceties that degrade gracefully:

- **Conditional create.** On an object store, `put()` with `ifNoneMatch` maps to
  `If-None-Match: *` so a concurrent uploader of identical bytes cannot clobber; a
  `412`/`409` is surfaced as a `false` return (re-`SELECT` + reuse), not an
  exception. On `local`/SQLite-test there is no conditional PUT, so it degrades to a
  best-effort `exists()` guard — the per-`(scope, sha256)` lock is the real
  serialiser there.
- **Server-side checksum.** On S3, `promote()` attaches
  `x-amz-checksum-sha256` (base64 of the raw digest) so S3 verifies the staged bytes;
  the local driver ignores it, so passing it is config-aware and safe.
- **Signed URLs.** `temporaryUrl()` mints a short-lived signed URL only on disks that
  support it (`providesTemporaryUrls()`); the `local`/SQLite-test disk returns
  `null` rather than throwing.

::: danger Keep the CAS bucket UNVERSIONED
The canonical CAS bucket must **not** use S3 lifecycle/versioning as a
blob-deletion mechanism. Vaulter's two-phase GC is the deletion authority; an S3
lifecycle rule deleting blobs out from under it will produce dangling rows. (A
lifecycle `AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload` rule for *resumable uploads* is a
different, recommended backstop — see the `uploads` config.)
:::
